Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
Diagnosis:
The failing test `testGetLineNumberWithCR()` constructs a CSVParser with input "a\rb\rc" and explicitly sets the line separator to "\r" (carriage return only). The test then asserts that the initial line number is 1.

The bug report points out an inconsistency in how line endings (EOL) are handled by ExtendedBufferedReader. Specifically, in the read() method, only '\n' (newline, LF) causes the lineCounter to increment:
```java
if (current == '\n') {
    lineCounter++;
}
```
But in readLine(), the superclass (BufferedReader) implementation is used, which treats CR, LF, and CRLF equivalently as line terminators but "drops them" from the returned line. ExtendedBufferedReader increments the lineCounter on every call to readLine(), regardless of what actual line separator was encountered:
```java
String line = super.readLine();
if (line != null) {
    ...
    lineCounter++;
}
```

The problem for the test is that the input uses only CR ('\r') as line separator, and ExtendedBufferedReader's read() does not count '\r' as a line break (only '\n'). Therefore, methods that rely on the lineCounter from read() will undercount lines when using CR line endings. The readLine() increments the counter correctly for each line regardless but this inconsistency can cause wrong line numbers in some usage sequences.

CSVParser.getLineNumber() calls lexer.getLineNumber(), which delegates to the underlying reader: `return in.getLineNumber();`. Here `in` is the ExtendedBufferedReader instance managing line counting.

Since the test verifies getLineNumber immediately after construction (line 510), the count reflects the line numbering logic which expects to handle "\r" as a line separator but currently does not in read().

The root cause is that ExtendedBufferedReader.read() increments lineCounter only on '\n', whereas to support "\r" line endings (as used by the test), it also needs to increment on '\r'. Without this fix, line number tracking is inconsistent and incorrect for inputs with CR line separators.

Hence, the bug arises from ExtendedBufferedReader not consistently recognizing CR as a valid end-of-line in its read() method, as the bug report states.

No other recent bug reports are relevant here.

# Summary:
- ExtendedBufferedReader.read() increments lineCounter only on '\n', ignoring '\r'.
- ExtendedBufferedReader.readLine() increments lineCounter unconditionally after BufferedReader.readLine().
- Test uses "\r" as line separator but line count is initially 1.
- Inconsistent EOL handling causes wrong line numbers.
- Fix is to handle '\r' in read() as well to increment line count.

This explains why the test for getLineNumberWithCR fails.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
